criteria_results.title: ISSUE_001: Temporal overbreadth objection for Request No. 3
criteria_results.reasoning: The response to Request No. 3 explicitly raises a temporal overbreadth objection, stating: 'The Agreement was negotiated in late 2020 and signed on January 15, 2021. The earliest alleged breach (the Northpoint relationship) arises in 2022--2023, and the Agreement expired on January 14, 2024. Distribution strategy from 2015 through mid-2020 predates any dealings under the Agreement by years and has no bearing on whether Redfield performed it.' The response proposes a narrowed period of July 1, 2020 through January 14, 2024 and explicitly states documents are being withheld on this basis.

Lakeshore did not begin buying V-Series units under the Agreement until January 15, 2021. Redfield proposes a period of January 1, 2020 through the present.' criteria_results.title: ISSUE_001: Temporal overbreadth objection for Request No. 11

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_001: Proposes narrowed time period for temporally overbroad requests

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_004: Addresses clawback mechanism for inadvertent disclosure
criteria_results.reasoning: Section V of the memo is entirely dedicated to the inadvertent production of REDFIELD-000847 (the Ng-Chen email of April 22, 2023). It also discusses the absence of a protective order or clawback stipulation, the waiver risk from delay, and the need to propose a stipulated protective order with a clawback/non-waiver clause. This thoroughly satisfies the criterion.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_004: Flags inadvertent disclosure as requiring immediate action

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_005: Trade secret/confidential info objection to Request No. 14
criteria_results.reasoning: The response to Request No. 14 explicitly raises a trade secret objection, citing MCL 445.1902, and states that V-Series engineering drawings, Bill of Materials data, and manufacturing processes are trade secrets. It also raises a relevance objection to manufacturing costs. The response withholds full-product drawings, Bill of Materials unrelated to the compressor-seal assembly, and manufacturing cost data, and designates produced documents as Attorneys' Eyes Only. This clearly satisfies the criterion of objecting on trade secret/confidential business information grounds as to manufacturing costs and Bill of Materials.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_005: Proposes protective order for Request No. 14 production
criteria_results.reasoning: The response to Request No. 14 explicitly states that documents produced under category (d) (design specifications, drawings, Bill of Materials entries, and engineering change orders for the compressor-seal assembly) 'will be designated Attorneys' Eyes Only under Section IV.' Section IV describes the protective order framework. The response also states Redfield is 'willing to meet and confer if Plaintiff can explain why it needs any withheld category.' This clearly proposes production subject to a protective order (Attorneys' Eyes Only designation) rather than outright refusal, satisfying the criterion.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_006: Identifies Slack/Teams preservation gap
criteria_results.reasoning: The memo clearly identifies the Slack/Teams preservation gap in Section IV. It states that the litigation hold issued on September 16, 2024 covered 'email, network drives, and local drives only' and that 'Slack (90-day auto-delete), Teams (1-year), and voicemail (60-day) retention settings were not suspended.' It further notes that the supplemental hold was not issued until November 1, 2024, and details the specific data lost during the gap period for both Slack (approximately 46 days of messages from June 18 to August 3, 2024) and Teams (messages from September 16 to November 1, 2023). This clearly satisfies the criterion.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_006: Identifies spoliation risk from Slack auto-delete policy
criteria_results.reasoning: The memo explicitly identifies the Slack auto-delete spoliation risk in Section IV. It states that Slack had a 90-day auto-delete policy, that the hold was issued September 16, 2024, and that by November 1 only messages from about August 3 forward remained. It calculates that messages from approximately June 18 to August 3, 2024 were auto-deleted during the 46 days after the hold issued, and flags this as post-hold data loss creating spoliation exposure. This directly satisfies the criterion.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_006: Notes David Kessler's team used Slack as primary platform
criteria_results.reasoning: The memo explicitly states in Section IV.A: 'Oct. 2024 - Custodian interviews reveal that Kessler, Morell, and Reeves used Slack as their primary internal channel.' This directly connects Kessler's reliance on Slack as the primary communication platform to the spoliation/preservation gap issue, satisfying the criterion.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_006: Recommends addressing completeness limitations in responses
criteria_results.reasoning: The memo extensively addresses the Slack/Teams preservation gap in Section IV. It recommends disclosing the preservation gap in the RFP responses (Section IV.C: 'Disclose. Instruction 7 asks for identification of lost documents... The draft includes a factual disclosure in Section III, with a reservation of rights on when the duty arose, and references it in RFP 6 and 22.'). It also recommends multiple supplemental preservation steps including forensic examination of devices for residual Slack data, collecting Kessler's phone, checking for Slack notification emails in Exchange, and offering additional custodians or search terms. The memo clearly satisfies the criterion by both recommending acknowledgment of completeness limitations in the responses and recommending supplemental preservation steps.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_007: Privacy objection to Request No. 21 (personnel files)
criteria_results.reasoning: The response to Request No. 21 explicitly raises a 'Non-party privacy' objection, stating that 'Complete personnel files contain medical information, benefits elections, tax forms, emergency contacts, and compensation history unrelated to this dispute, all of which are protected by the privacy interests of non-party employees.' criteria_results.title: ISSUE_007: Offers narrowed production of relevant personnel file content
criteria_results.reasoning: The response to Request No. 21 explicitly limits production to specific categories of personnel file content directly relevant to the claims: (a) job descriptions and scope of authority, (b) dates of employment and position history, (c) organizational reporting lines, (d) employment agreements, (e) sales-incentive/commission/bonus plan documents tied to Lakeshore, Northpoint, or V-Series sales, and (f) performance evaluations or disciplinary records addressing handling of the Lakeshore/Northpoint accounts or V-Series quality issues. It expressly withholds the remainder of personnel files (medical information, benefits, tax forms, etc.) as irrelevant and privacy-protected. This is a narrowed production of relevant portions rather than either a blanket refusal or production of entire files.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_008: Objection to Request No. 24 as improper contention discovery
criteria_results.reasoning: The response to Request No. 24 explicitly raises the contention-discovery objection. It states: 'The Request asks Redfield to sort and marshal its evidence by legal theory. MCR 2.310 requires production of documents described by category, not organization of evidence by the requesting party's view of the defenses. Contention discovery belongs in interrogatories under MCR 2.309, served at an appropriate stage. It is premature now, before any depositions have been taken and before Redfield's review is complete.' This directly satisfies the criterion by objecting that the request is an improper contention request disguised as a document request, that it improperly seeks to compel marshaling of evidence by legal theory, and that such discovery belongs in contention interrogatories and is premature.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_009: Proportionality objection to Request No. 6 (all ESI)
criteria_results.reasoning: The response to Request No. 6 raises an overbreadth objection regarding 'any' Redfield employee, noting that searching every employee's mailbox would impose 'substantial burden with little benefit.' However, the criterion specifically asks whether a proportionality objection is raised referencing MCR 2.302(B)(1) or proportionality principles. The response does not cite MCR 2.302(B)(1) or explicitly use the word 'proportionality' in the Request No. 6 response. It frames the objection as 'overbreadth as to persons' and mentions 'substantial burden with little benefit,' which is a proportionality concept, but does not explicitly invoke proportionality principles or MCR 2.302(B)(1). The criterion requires referencing 'the burden of the request relative to the needs of the case, or citing MCR 2.302(B)(1) or proportionality principles.' The phrase 'substantial burden with little benefit' does reference burden relative to benefit/needs, which is the essence of proportionality. This is sufficient to satisfy the criterion as described.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_009: Proposes reasonable limitations on ESI production
criteria_results.reasoning: The response to Request No. 6 proposes multiple reasonable limitations on ESI production: (1) limiting custodians to the twelve identified individuals rather than searching all hundreds of Redfield employees; (2) noting that voicemail is unavailable (per Section III); (3) noting that Slack communications with Lakeshore are not believed to exist; (4) limiting the search to specific shared drives (Sales, Operations, Finance, Executive). The response explicitly states documents are being withheld in part because non-custodian employee communications are not being searched, and explains the proportionality rationale. These are reasonable, well-articulated limitations on ESI scope.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_009: References Michigan proportionality factors or MCR 2.302(B)(1)
criteria_results.reasoning: The RFP response to Request No. 6 explicitly invokes MCR 2.302(B)(1) proportionality in the General Objections (General Objection 3 references 'not proportional to the needs of the case under MCR 2.302(B)(1)'). Additionally, the response to Request No. 9 explicitly raises 'Proportionality' as a heading and discusses burden vs. benefit ('Reviewing all nationwide distributor communications over five years would require searching the mailboxes of the entire sales and customer-service organization... at a cost disproportionate to the issues in this case'). The response to Request No. 6 itself cites the overbreadth objection referencing 'substantial burden with little benefit,' which tracks proportionality factors. MCR 2.302(B)(1) is cited by name in General Objection 3, which is incorporated into the specific responses. This satisfies the criterion.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_010: Work product objection to Request No. 22 (litigation hold memo)
criteria_results.reasoning: The response to Request No. 22 explicitly asserts work product protection for the litigation hold memoranda, stating: 'The litigation hold memoranda were prepared at the direction of counsel. Parts of them reflect counsel's mental impressions about anticipated claims, key issues, and preservation scope (opinion work product under MCR 2.302(B)(3)).' This directly satisfies the criterion requiring a work product objection based on counsel's mental impressions about anticipated claims and key custodians.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_010: Distinguishes fact vs. opinion work product for litigation hold
criteria_results.reasoning: The response to Request No. 22 explicitly states: 'Parts of them reflect counsel's mental impressions about anticipated claims, key issues, and preservation scope (opinion work product under MCR 2.302(B)(3)).' This directly characterizes the litigation hold memoranda as containing opinion work product. The issues memo (Section IV.C) also references 'opinion work product' in the context of the hold notices and states they will be produced 'with opinion work product redacted.' The distinction between fact and opinion work product is drawn in the RFP response itself, which cites MCR 2.302(B)(3) and notes that Redfield will produce the hold notices with opinion work product redacted while producing factual information about preservation efforts. This satisfies the criterion.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_010: Acknowledges fact of litigation hold may be discoverable
criteria_results.reasoning: The response to Request No. 22 explicitly distinguishes between the litigation hold memoranda (which are protected as work product/privilege) and the factual information about preservation efforts (which is discoverable). Specifically, it states it will produce: (a) the hold notices with opinion work product redacted, (b) the list of recipients and custodian acknowledgment forms, (c) documents showing data sources covered and dates automatic deletion was suspended, (d) retention settings in effect, and (e) non-privileged communications with IT personnel. The response also offers a stipulation or deposition under MCR 2.306(B)(5) concerning preservation efforts. The issues memo similarly distinguishes between the privileged content of hold memoranda and the discoverable facts about preservation, noting that hold notices will be produced with opinion work product redacted. This clearly acknowledges that the fact of the litigation hold, its timing, scope, recipients, and implementation details are discoverable, while only the attorney mental impressions embedded in the memoranda are protected.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_003: Distinguishes Ng April 22 email from other vague entries
criteria_results.reasoning: The memo treats the April 22, 2023 Ng email (REDFIELD-000847) separately from the other pre-retention entries. In Section V, it analyzes REDFIELD-000847 in detail, noting it explicitly references privilege and outside counsel, and provides a model redescription that highlights its stronger privilege foundation. In Section VI.B, when discussing the pre-retention Chen/Ng entries (1, 3–7), the memo notes these six entries have only vague descriptions like 'Discussion of quality testing results' and are insufficient, recommending re-review and possible production. The memo explicitly uses Entry 2 (REDFIELD-000847) as the model for how to properly describe a privileged document, implicitly distinguishing it from the other six. However, the memo does not explicitly state in Section VI.B that Entry 2 has a stronger privilege foundation than entries 1 and 3–7 — it treats Entry 2 separately in Section V and the other six in Section VI.B, but the distinction is implicit rather than explicit. The criterion asks whether the memo 'distinguishes' the April 22 email from the other 6 entries, recognizing its stronger privilege foundation. The memo does treat them differently: Entry 2 gets detailed analysis in Section V with a model description showing strong privilege, while entries 1 and 3–7 are flagged as vulnerable in Section VI.B. The memo references 'the Entry 2 model in Section V' when discussing how to redescribe the other entries, which implicitly acknowledges Entry 2 has a stronger foundation. This constitutes a meaningful distinction between the April 22 email and the other six entries.

criteria_results.title: Memo cross-references privilege log deficiency with inadvertent disclosure
